summary: This paper preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory audit of deterministic contamination detectors on a 150‑item NetOps sample using a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic NetOps validator. Execution artifacts show zero high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded), producing a degenerate paired outcome (no discordant pairs). The run is well‑archived and the Disclosure Statement present, but the experiment's design choices (provenance‑stable synthetic sampling + shared_initial_candidate generation semantics producing one shared model call per item) materially limited the confirmatory test's ability to detect contamination effects and thus the manuscript must more strongly acknowledge and quantify these limitations and improve scholarly framing.
critical_issues: Primary confirmatory test is effectively uninformative given execution: independent_condition_generation=false produced a single shared model generation per item, so baseline vs guarded used identical outputs unless an exclusion triggered; this makes the paired test unable to detect generation-level differences and undermines H2 as a confirmatory hypothesis unless this degeneracy is made explicit and reframed.

The sampled items for this execution were provenance‑stable synthetic/generated tasks (source_identifier:"synthetic-netops:"), not public/web‑sourced benchmark items. That sampling choice (though allowed by the preregistration) substantially limits the manuscript's audit claim about contamination prevalence in public benchmarks and must be stated prominently (abstract, intro, and limitations).

The manuscript currently contains heavy artifact/hash listing and provenance bookkeeping inside the main narrative, which gives an artifact‑report feel rather than concise, literature‑grounded scholarly prose; this reduces readability and may violate conference prose expectations.

The paper reports zero high‑confidence flags but does not present summary statistics of the fuzzy 5‑gram overlap distribution or minimum/median overlap distances to the preregistered thresholds; without those summaries the reader cannot assess whether the zero flags reflect genuinely distant items or threshold choices.

Some claims about the experiment being a confirmatory paired test are misleading given the two execution facts above (synthetic sampling + shared generation). The manuscript needs to explicitly qualify any language claiming a confirmatory test outcome and must avoid implying broader generality to public benchmarks or to multi‑model settings.
required_revisions: Add an explicit, prominent statement (abstract and end of Introduction) that the executed sample was deterministically generated synthetic items and that independent_condition_generation=false produced shared model outputs per item, and therefore the preregistered paired confirmatory test was degenerate/uninformative for detecting generation‑level contamination effects in this run. Cite the specific archived artifacts (task_manifest SHA and model_configuration SHA) already recorded in the bundle to support this statement.

Replace or substantially shorten provenance/hash‑heavy narrative in the main text; convert the long lists of artifact hashes and execution manifest items into a concise one‑paragraph summary and a single compact table (or very short appendix paragraph), and explicitly state that the full manifest and raw artifacts are archived in the execution bundle (reference artifact paths/SHA prefixes). This is a text edit that can be resolved from the supplied artifacts.

Report summary statistics (and a short figure/table) of the fuzzy 5‑gram overlap scores computed for all sampled items versus the public corpus fingerprints used by the detector (e.g., min, median, 75th percentile, and maximum overlap), and report how far items were from the preregistered high‑confidence threshold (≥0.80). These numbers should be derivable from the archived contamination detection outputs and raw overlap scores.

Revise the Results and Conclusion wording to avoid implying that the audit found evidence about contamination prevalence in web‑sourced/public NetOps benchmarks. Explicitly limit the paper's inferential scope to the executed synthetic sample and describe precisely which (preregistered) questions were answered and which remain untested by this execution.

In Methods and Threats to Validity, add a focused paragraph explaining how the preregistered choices (deterministic generator allowed by the preregistration and shared_initial_candidate semantics) produced the observed outcome, why these choices were compliant with the preregistration, and how they reduce power and informativeness for the primary estimand. Point readers to the deterministic_reconciliation artifact and paired_contingency_table SHA for verification.
optional_revisions: For readability, move one representative short exemplar artifact (e.g., one task manifest entry and its matched raw response + validator trace) into a very short boxed example in the main paper and move remaining examples to the archived bundle; this preserves clarity while avoiding main‑text provenance overload.

Add a short summary paragraph in Related Work that more directly contrasts prior contamination audits on web‑sourced benchmarks vs this synthetic sampling audit, to better position contributions and limitations.

If space permits, include a brief sensitivity paragraph quantifying how the paired test's detectable effect size would change under independent_condition_generation and/or multi‑model sampling (use the preregistered power curves already described in the preregistration artifacts rather than new model calls).
